strengths: The paper proposes a compelling and timely direction: replacing finite pixel-history memories with a persistent learned 3D state for interactive world models. The decomposition into world-frame dynamics, camera prediction, projection, and learned pixel rendering is well motivated and technically coherent.

The method is described in considerable architectural detail, including VAE designs, denoiser/camera hyperparameters, inference algorithms, sampler settings, dataset scale, and compute requirements. This makes the core system easier to reason about than many comparable world-model papers.

The qualitative capabilities enabled by explicit 3D state are interesting and plausibly valuable: single-image 3D world initialization, explicit 3D conditioning, mid-rollout world edits, and off-screen dynamics that continue to evolve.

The evaluation includes both FVD and a human study targeting visual fidelity, spatial consistency, temporal consistency, and overall quality. The reported gains for PERSIST variants over the included baselines are large, and the limitations section is unusually candid about ground-truth 3D supervision, exposure bias, finite spatial memory, and long-rollout glitches.
weaknesses: The central comparative evidence is weakened by a serious baseline comparability issue. PERSIST is evaluated in Craftium/Luanti, while Oasis and WorldMem are evaluated on a separate MineDojo/Minecraft evaluation set because the baselines were trained on Minecraft data. Thus the headline FVD and user-study comparisons mix model differences with domain, renderer, dataset, and policy differences. This makes the claim that PERSIST substantially outperforms existing methods less firmly supported than the tables suggest.

There is no clean same-data ablation isolating the contribution of persistent 3D state. The paper states that Oasis can be viewed as disabling the 3D guidance, but it is not trained/evaluated under the same Craftium setup. Important missing ablations include a Craftium-trained pixel-only AR model, a same-backbone memory-retrieval model, variants without camera prediction or without world-to-pixel projection, and comparisons at matched compute/context budgets.

The evaluation relies heavily on subjective ratings from 28 participants and about 800 rollout evaluations, but the statistical treatment is thin. The paper reports means and errors and says methods significantly outperform baselines, yet does not clearly specify statistical tests, participant/video random effects, inter-rater reliability, blinding details, or whether paired comparisons were analyzed with an appropriate model.

The method requires supervised access to dense 3D voxel world-frames and camera states during training. This is honestly acknowledged, but it substantially narrows applicability beyond simulators or annotated 3D datasets and makes the framing as a general paradigm for interactive world models somewhat ahead of the evidence.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters and algorithms are detailed, but I did not find a code, checkpoint, dataset, or evaluation-interface release statement. Given the very large training cost, reproducing the main results would be difficult without released artifacts.

The ethics/impact discussion is minimal. While the synthetic-domain setting lowers immediate risk, interactive generative world models can plausibly affect game/content production, simulation-based agent training, and synthetic data pipelines; the paper does not discuss misuse, dataset provenance/licensing, or risks from training agents in learned simulators.

strengths: The core idea of replacing pixel-history retrieval with an explicitly persistent 3D latent state is well motivated for interactive world models, and the decomposition into world-frame prediction, camera prediction, and world-to-pixel rendering is conceptually appealing.

The paper contains substantial engineering detail, including model/component descriptions, inference algorithms, hyperparameters, and a limitations section that honestly discusses dependence on 3D supervision, exposure bias, and bounded spatial memory.
The qualitative capabilities enabled by the representation, such as 3D initialization, mid-episode world edits, and off-screen dynamics, are interesting and potentially useful if made robust.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is not convincing. The main baselines, Oasis and WorldMem, are evaluated under different domain/training conditions: the paper says PERSIST is trained/evaluated on Craftium/Luanti, while baselines are evaluated on MineDojo to match their Minecraft training. This makes the headline Table 1 comparison difficult to interpret as a controlled method comparison.

The central contribution relies on privileged ground-truth 3D voxel observations and camera states during training. This is acknowledged, but it greatly narrows applicability and weakens claims about a general world-modeling paradigm. The paper does not show learning the 3D state from pixels or evaluate outside voxel-game settings.

The baselines are insufficient for isolating the contribution. There is no clearly matched pixel-only baseline trained on the same 40M interactions with comparable compute, no ablation of the projected 3D conditioning versus extra model capacity, and no careful comparison to simpler state-conditioned or depth/semantic-conditioned variants.

The evaluation evidence is too thin for the strength of the claims. FVD is reported across corresponding datasets rather than a single shared distribution, the user study has only 28 participants, and the paper provides limited statistical analysis beyond mean ± error values. Many claimed capabilities are shown qualitatively rather than measured.

The method is extremely expensive and complex, involving multiple separately trained large models and VAEs, yet reproducibility is incomplete: the paper gives hyperparameters but does not appear to provide code, data, pretrained checkpoints, or enough low-level details to reproduce the data collection, user study, or training pipeline reliably.

Long-horizon stability remains unresolved. The appendix shows object disappearance, hallucinated blocks, texture drift, and collision failures in a 2000-step rollout; this undercuts the paper's stronger claims about coherent evolving 3D worlds, especially for agent-training use cases.

The impact/ethics discussion is superficial. Interactive generative environments can affect embodied-agent training, simulation reliability, user-generated content, and misuse through synthetic interactive media, but the paper largely dismisses risks because experiments are synthetic.

strengths: The paper proposes a compelling and timely shift from pixel-history autoregression to an explicit persistent latent 3D state for interactive world models. The decomposition into world-frame prediction, camera prediction, geometric projection, and learned pixel rendering is conceptually clean and well motivated by the failure modes of rolling-window and key-frame memory methods.

The method is technically substantial. PERSIST combines 3D latent dynamics, differentiable voxel projection/depth peeling, camera-conditioned generation, and diffusion/flow-based autoregressive prediction in a coherent pipeline. The 3D state also enables useful capabilities beyond standard video rollout quality, including 3D initialization, mid-episode world editing, and off-screen dynamics.

The empirical results are promising: PERSIST variants substantially outperform Oasis and WorldMem in reported FVD and human ratings, with especially clear gains in temporal stability and 3D consistency. The evaluation includes long rollouts, held-out procedurally generated worlds, multiple action policies, qualitative examples, and an 800+ video user study.

The manuscript is clearly written and unusually honest about limitations. It explicitly discusses reliance on ground-truth 3D supervision, exposure bias, finite spatial memory, and remaining gap to ground-truth rollouts, which helps calibrate the contribution rather than oversell it.

Implementation details are fairly extensive, including model sizes, context windows, latent resolutions, training compute, inference sampler settings, and user-study protocol, which supports partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The strongest concern is evaluation comparability. PERSIST is trained/evaluated in Craftium/Luanti, while Oasis and WorldMem are evaluated on a separate MineDojo/Minecraft setup to avoid domain shift for those baselines. This makes the headline cross-method comparison less clean: differences may reflect data, environment, policy, implementation, or training distribution rather than only persistent 3D state.

The main baselines are not matched ablations trained under the same data, compute, and architecture conditions. The paper notes Oasis can be viewed as disabling 3D guidance, but because the baseline comparison is not in the same environment/training regime, the causal evidence for the 3D state would be stronger with same-data ablations such as removing projection guidance, replacing 3D memory with longer pixel memory, using ground-truth camera only, or varying world-frame supervision.

The approach currently depends on supervised access to dense 3D voxel state and camera state during training. This is acknowledged, but it substantially narrows applicability relative to the broad claims about learned world models from data and limits transfer to real video or simulators without privileged state.

The user study is useful but still somewhat underspecified for statistical strength. The paper reports mean ± uncertainty and head-to-head matrices, but does not clearly describe participant expertise, randomization/blinding details, inter-rater reliability, or statistical tests for the central claims.

Reproducibility remains challenging despite good hyperparameter reporting. The system requires very large training data, multiple large models, many GPU-days on A100/H100 hardware, and likely nontrivial game-engine/data-collection infrastructure. There is no clear statement about code, datasets, trained checkpoints, or evaluation videos being released.

The strongest reported configuration, PERSIST-XL+w0, uses ground-truth 3D initialization, which is informative but less comparable to single-image initialization. Some of the best numbers therefore rely on extra privileged information at inference time, and this should be separated more carefully from the default setting in the claims.

The method still exhibits autoregressive drift and local 3D-state errors over long horizons. The appendix examples are reassuring in showing recovery, but the central claims about long-horizon stability would be stronger with quantitative degradation curves over time rather than aggregate scores over fixed-length clips.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and compelling idea: replacing finite pixel-history conditioning with an explicitly maintained latent 3D world state, coupled to camera prediction and a learned renderer. This is a meaningful architectural direction for long-horizon interactive world models.

The empirical gains over pixel-history baselines are substantial in the reported setting. FVD remains far more stable over 200/400/600 frames, and the human study consistently favors PERSIST variants for visual fidelity, 3D consistency, temporal consistency, and overall quality.

The paper includes useful ablations, including smaller 3D denoiser, no 3D upscaling, ground-truth camera conditioning, and explicit initial 3D state conditioning. These help isolate which components matter and show that the persistent 3D representation is doing real work.

Presentation is generally strong. The decomposition into world-frame prediction, camera prediction, projection, and pixel generation is understandable, figures are informative, and the appendix provides model sizes, inference logic, human-study protocol, and inference-speed breakdowns.

The limitations section is unusually candid and relevant: the authors explicitly discuss dependence on ground-truth 3D supervision, exposure bias, finite spatial memory, and lack of real-time inference.
weaknesses: The central limitation is that the method depends on supervised 3D world-frame labels during training, here from a voxel game engine. This substantially narrows the contribution relative to the broad framing of learned world models from data, and it is unclear how well the approach transfers to real video or environments without simulator-state access.

The evaluation domain is narrow: all main results are in a Minecraft/Luanti-like voxel environment where the representation is naturally aligned with the engine state. This makes the 3D-state approach attractive but also leaves open whether the method works in non-voxel, continuous, visually complex, or physics-rich environments.

The comparison to baselines has some caveats. Quantitative baselines are trained under a shared formulation, but the human study uses released Oasis/WorldMem models on a separate Minedojo setup because it was conducted before retraining. The authors attempt to check domain bias, but this still weakens the cleanliness of the subjective comparison.

Claims about persistent dynamics and off-screen causal effects are mostly supported by qualitative examples rather than systematic metrics. There is no direct evaluation of 3D-state accuracy, collision consistency, object permanence, or off-screen dynamics beyond selected demonstrations.

The system is extremely computationally heavy: multiple large components, hundreds of millions of parameters, 40M interactions, long multi-GPU training, and around 2.7 seconds per generated frame for PERSIST-S with 20 denoising steps. This limits practical interactivity and reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameters.

The method is assembled from separately trained components and still suffers from exposure bias and long-horizon artifacts, as acknowledged by the authors. The lack of end-to-end rollout training or stronger robustness evaluation leaves some uncertainty about reliability over truly open-ended interaction.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript alone. Architecture and training details are extensive, but there is no clear indication of code, trained models, dataset release, or exact data-generation scripts, and reproducing the main results would require very substantial compute and simulator instrumentation.

strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of current interactive video/world models: finite pixel-history context and poor long-horizon spatial consistency. The proposed decomposition into a persistent latent 3D world frame, camera model, projection operator, and pixel renderer is a clear and plausible architectural direction.

The empirical setup is more substantial than many papers in this area: the authors collect a large Luanti/Craftium dataset, compare against Oasis and WorldMem-style pixel-history baselines, include several ablations, report FVD/FID over 600-frame rollouts, and run a human study with over 800 video evaluations.

The method enables genuinely interesting capabilities that are hard to obtain from pixel-only histories, including explicit 3D initialization, mid-rollout 3D edits, and examples of off-screen dynamics affecting later observations.

The limitations section is unusually candid about key constraints: reliance on ground-truth 3D supervision, finite local spatial memory, exposure bias, and lack of real-time inference. These are material limitations but they are at least acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central contribution is less general than the framing suggests. PERSIST depends on supervised access to simulator-provided 3D voxel world frames and camera states during training, which makes the method much closer to learning a neural renderer/dynamics model for an instrumented voxel simulator than a broadly applicable world model from pixels. This substantially limits significance beyond Minecraft-like synthetic environments.

The evidence for persistent 3D state as the decisive factor is incomplete. The main metrics are FVD/FID and human ratings, but there are no direct quantitative measurements of 3D state accuracy, camera accuracy, spatial memory under controlled revisits, collision correctness, off-screen dynamics, or edit fidelity. Many of the most distinctive claims are supported mostly by qualitative examples.

The evaluation is narrow and potentially fragile. All experiments are in a single voxel-game domain with scripted/random action policies; there is no demonstration on non-voxel 3D data, real video, embodied control, downstream agent training, or more diverse interaction regimes. The paper claims broad relevance to interactive world simulation, but the empirical scope is much more specialized.

The human study comparison is not fully clean: Appendix B states that it used released Oasis/WorldMem models trained on Minecraft-style data and separate Minedojo evaluation sets, rather than the same retrained baselines/domain used in the quantitative evaluation. The authors try to justify this via ground-truth preference checks, but generated-model comparisons across different domains and training setups remain a confound.

The baseline and ablation suite leaves important questions unanswered. It does not compare to simpler privileged-state baselines, such as conditioning a pixel model directly on projected ground-truth or predicted semantic voxels, a deterministic/neural renderer from voxel state, stronger retrieval with more memory, or an oracle world-state variant over full rollouts. This makes it hard to isolate how much benefit comes from the proposed learned persistent state versus privileged 3D supervision and projection.

Practicality is weak despite the speed discussion. The model requires multiple large components, around weeks of A100/H100 training, and inference is roughly 2.7 seconds per frame for PERSIST-S at 20 denoising steps, or about 1.13 FPS in the fast setting. This is far from the interactive use case emphasized in the introduction.

Presentation and reproducibility are uneven. The architecture tables are useful, but the manuscript does not clearly commit to releasing code, data, trained models, prompts/interfaces, evaluation videos, or exact evaluation scripts. Some references/years appear corrupted or placeholder-like, and several claims in the text are stronger than the reported evidence supports.

The impact statement is too shallow. Synthetic-domain work can still affect game generation, simulation, embodied AI evaluation, and downstream decision-making; simply stating that no immediate negative societal consequences are foreseen does not adequately discuss misuse, bias in generated simulations, or risks from training agents in inaccurate learned environments.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and compelling shift from pixel-history memories to a persistent latent 3D world state for interactive world models. The decomposition into world-frame prediction, camera prediction, projection, and learned pixel rendering is well motivated and technically coherent.

Empirical results are strong within the chosen domain: PERSIST substantially improves FVD over Oasis and WorldMem across 200/400/600-frame rollouts, and its FID remains stable while pixel-history baselines degrade over time.

The evaluation includes useful ablations, including smaller 3D denoisers, no 3D upscaling, ground-truth camera conditioning, and explicit initial 3D state conditioning. These support the central claim that persistent 3D structure is doing real work.

The human study directly targets visual fidelity, 3D consistency, temporal consistency, and overall quality, complementing FVD/FID and aligning with the paper’s central concerns about long-horizon coherence.

The manuscript is well organized and unusually transparent about limitations: dependence on supervised 3D state, exposure bias, finite spatial memory, and lack of real-time inference are all discussed concretely.

The method enables interesting capabilities beyond metric gains, including 3D initialization, mid-episode 3D edits, and off-screen dynamics, which strengthen the significance of the representation choice.
weaknesses: The main limitation is substantial: training requires ground-truth 3D voxel state and camera information from a simulator. This restricts applicability to instrumented environments and makes the broader framing around general world models somewhat stronger than the demonstrated setting supports.

The experimental domain is narrow: results are only shown in a Minecraft/Luanti-like voxel world. It remains unclear how well the approach transfers to more visually complex, non-voxel, deformable, or real-world environments.

Some of the most exciting claims, such as persistent off-screen dynamics and emergent causal effects, are demonstrated mainly qualitatively. More targeted quantitative tests of spatial memory, collision consistency, edit fidelity, and off-screen state evolution would make the evidence stronger.

The human-study comparison is not perfectly aligned with the main quantitative setup: the appendix notes that released Oasis/WorldMem models were evaluated on a separate Minedojo domain for the study, while later quantitative comparisons use models trained on the authors’ data. This is explained, but it still complicates interpretation.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper provides many architectural and training details, but the system is large, computationally expensive, and depends on a custom data pipeline; without released code, trained models, or dataset generation scripts, independent reproduction would be difficult.
The method is far from real time, even with the reported speedups. This weakens claims about interactive deployment, although the authors are appropriately candid about it.
